79:1.title: The Opening Oaths of An-Nāziʿāt
79:1.in_short: The surah opens with a string of oaths sworn by unnamed pullers, loosers, swimmers, racers and managers. Almost every classical voice takes them as angels at the moment of death, though several also read them as death itself, the stars, bows, ships, or racing horses, and all agree the final one, the 'managers of affairs', are angels.

claims.text: A widely reported early view (going back to Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq and Mujahid) is that the nāziʿāt are simply angels who pull out the souls of the children of Adam in general, without specifying disbelievers.

sources.original_excerpt: هم الملائكة التي تنـزع نفوس بني آدم

claims.text: Most later commentators specify the nāziʿāt as the angels of punishment who wrench out the souls of disbelievers harshly, 'as though drowning', in contrast to the gentle nāshiṭāt who draw out believers' souls.

sources.original_excerpt: يعني الملائكة تنزع أرواح الكفار من أجسادهم

original_terms.gloss: those who pull out / wrench out

claims.text: An alternative reading holds that the nāziʿāt is death itself, which pulls the soul out of the person.

sources.original_excerpt: الموت ينـزع النفوس

claims.text: Another reading takes the nāziʿāt as the stars, which sink from one horizon and rise from another.
Others held the nāziʿāt to be bows, drawn back to their fullest extent to loose an arrow.
Al-Suddi read the nāziʿāt as the soul itself, at the moment it drowns within the chest as death approaches.

sources.original_excerpt: النفس حين تَغرق في الصدر

claims.text: A further reading, traced to Yahya ibn Sallam, takes the nāziʿāt as wild game bolting away in fright.
The word gharqan is a verbal noun standing for ighrāq, meaning to exert oneself to the very limit, as an archer draws a bow to its fullest stretch before releasing the arrow.

sources.original_excerpt: أغرق في القوس أي استوفى مدها

original_terms.gloss: utmost exertion, drawn to the limit (from ighrāq)

claims.text: Al-Ṭabarī's own conclusion is that God did not restrict the oath to one referent: every 'puller' that pulls in this manner, whether angel, death, star, bow, or anything else, is swept into the oath.

sources.original_excerpt: فكلّ نازعة غرقا، فداخلة في قسمه

claims.text: The nāshiṭāt are widely taken as angels who draw out believers' souls gently and easily, like untying a hobbling-rope from a camel's leg, in contrast with the violence of the nāziʿāt.

sources.original_excerpt: تنشِط نفس المؤمن فتقبضُها، كما ينشط العقال من البعير

original_terms.gloss: to loosen a knot easily, release without a struggle

claims.text: Israr Ahmad relays a saying attributed to the Prophet ﷺ that when the believer's soul is taken it feels like a single drop falling from a sealed waterskin, whereas the disbeliever's soul is pulled like meat torn off a skewer.
Al-Saʿdī also raises the possibility that the assignment could run the other way: that the forceful pulling belongs to believers' souls and the gentle loosening to disbelievers' souls.

sources.original_excerpt: أو أن النزع يكون لأرواح المؤمنين، والنشط لأرواح الكفار

claims.text: Alternative readings of the nāshiṭāt include: death itself; the stars moving from horizon to horizon; snares or lassoes used to catch game; and wild oxen roaming eagerly from place to place, supported by pre-Islamic verse.
Ibn 'Abbas is also reported to have read the nāshiṭāt as the believer's own soul, eager to leave the body because Paradise has already been shown to it before death.

Some held that the first two oaths together belong to the disbelievers alone, described first as forced out and then as torn out in anguish, while the next pair of oaths belongs to believers departing the world.
The sābiḥāt are generally taken as angels who glide or 'swim' swiftly, descending from heaven and ascending back to carry out God's command.

original_terms.gloss: to swim or glide swiftly

claims.text: One report takes the sābiḥāt as death, which spreads or 'swims' through the human soul.
Others took the sābiḥāt as the stars, sun and moon swimming in their orbits, linking it to the Qur'anic phrase 'each in an orbit swims' (21:33).
'Ata' read the sābiḥāt as ships gliding upon water.
A further reading takes the sābiḥāt as war-horses racing into battle, supported with lines of pre-Islamic verse by 'Antara and Imru' al-Qays describing horses that 'swim' at full gallop.

The sābiqāt are mostly taken as angels racing ahead, variously explained as outracing Satan to deliver revelation to the prophets before it can be stolen, racing to record good deeds, or racing to carry believers' souls to Paradise.
Alternative readings of the sābiqāt include death outracing the human being; war-horses that race; and the stars outracing one another in their courses.
Ibn Mas'ud and al-Rabi' are reported to have read the sābiqāt as the souls of believers themselves, racing eagerly toward the angels who will take them, having already glimpsed the joy awaiting them.

Al-Qushayrī is cited as saying scholars are agreed that the mudabbirāt are angels who manage and administer affairs by God's command, though the true management belongs to God and is only attributed to them by way of the created causes He employs.

sources.original_excerpt: أجمعوا على أن المراد الملائكة

original_terms.gloss: those who manage or administer an affair

claims.text: A minority view, reported from Mu'adh ibn Jabal via Khalid ibn Ma'dan, held that the mudabbirāt could be the seven celestial bodies, whose rising and setting God has tied to changes in worldly conditions, so that management is named after them though it belongs to God alone.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit is reported to have specified four angels who manage the world's affairs: Jibril, in charge of wind and armies; Mika'il, in charge of rain and vegetation; the Angel of Death, in charge of seizing souls; and Israfil, who delivers the command to them.

Al-Sa'di describes the mudabbirāt more broadly as angels entrusted with much of the management of both the upper and lower worlds: rain, plants, trees, winds, seas, embryos, animals, Paradise and Hellfire.

Mufti Shafi' links the mudabbirāt to a final task of the angels of death: arranging the means of reward and comfort for deserving souls, or of punishment and pain for wrongdoers, locating this reward and punishment in the grave (barzakh), citing a lengthy tradition of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib found in Mishkat al-Masabih via Musnad Ahmad.

report.graded_by: Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (source does not state a grade)

claims.text: Israr Ahmad reads the mudabbirāt as the angels who carry each departing soul, as commanded, to Sijjīn or 'Illiyyīn.

original_terms.gloss: the register or place of the wicked / the register or place of the righteous

claims.text: The response to this oath (the jawāb al-qasam) is left unstated in the wording; commentators supply it as an affirmation that resurrection and reckoning will certainly happen, on the pattern of similar oath-openings elsewhere in the Qur'an, while some instead locate the stated response later in the verse 'truly in that is a lesson for whoever fears.'

Al-Tanṭāwī, citing al-Zamakhshari and al-Shawkani, and noting this as closer to what is transmitted from many companions and successors, holds that all five descriptions most likely name one single group at different tasks: the angels, rather than a mixture of angels, stars, ships and horses.

Sayyid Qutb reflects that whatever the precise referents of these oaths, the Qur'an's purpose here is to stir human awareness and put the listener on alert for the coming great event described next, and that pressing for exact identification of each word is unnecessary, citing 'Umar's remark that not knowing the meaning of every single word will not bring down the Day of Judgement.

Wahiduddin Khan reads the passage against the yearly natural cycle: calm weather followed by storm-bearing winds and rain, after which desolate land bursts into new green growth, taken as a symbolic pointer to the possibility of the Hereafter emerging from the present world.

79:1.essay_html:
The surah opens with five oaths sworn by unnamed pullers, loosers, swimmers, racers and managers, and the text never says outright who or what they are. The largest body of commentators, going back to companions such as Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, takes them as angels engaged with the human soul at the moment of death.1,4 Many later commentators sharpen this into a contrast: the nāziʿāt ("those who pull out") are angels who wrench the souls of disbelievers out harshly, 'as though drowning', while the nāshiṭāt ("those who loosen") draw believers' souls out gently, like untying a rope from a camel's leg.2,3,5,7,8,9,11,12,13,14 Israr Ahmad relays a saying that the believer's soul departs like a single drop from a sealed skin, while the disbeliever's is torn out like meat off a skewer.8 Al-Sa'di, unusually, also allows the reverse assignment as a possibility.5

Alongside this main reading sit several others reported by the earlier exegetes. The nāziʿāt have also been read as death itself pulling out the soul, as the stars sinking and rising from horizon to horizon, as bows drawn to their fullest stretch, as the soul drowning within its own chest, or even as wild game bolting in fright.1,2,3,6 The word gharqan ("drowning") is explained linguistically as a verbal noun for ighrāq, meaning to exert oneself to the very limit, as an archer draws a bow as far as it will go.1,2,3,7,9 Al-Tabari's own judgement, after surveying all these reports, is that God did not restrict the oath to one referent: whatever pulls in this manner, angel or death or star or bow, is swept into it.1 The nāshiṭāt likewise carry alternative readings: death, the stars, snares for catching game, or wild oxen roaming eagerly, drawn from pre-Islamic poetry.1,2,3,6 Ibn 'Abbas is also reported to have read it as the believer's own soul, eager to leave the body once Paradise is shown to it before death.3

The third oath, the sābiḥāt ("those who swim"), is generally read as angels gliding swiftly between heaven and earth to carry out God's command.1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,11,12,13,14 Others took it as death spreading through the soul, as the stars, sun and moon swimming in their orbits, echoing the verse 'each in an orbit swims', as ships gliding on water, or as war-horses racing into battle, backed by lines of old Arabic verse.1,2,3,9 The fourth oath, the sābiqāt ("those who race ahead"), is mostly read as angels outracing Satan so revelation reaches the prophets unstolen, or racing to record good deeds, or racing to carry believers' souls to Paradise, though death, racehorses, the stars, and even the eager souls of believers themselves are also reported as possible referents.2,3,5,7,11,12,14

The fifth oath stands apart. Al-Qushayri is cited as saying the commentators are agreed that the mudabbirāt ("those who manage the affair") are angels, though the true management belongs to God and is only named after them as the means He employs.1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,11,12,13,14 One report names four angels for this task: Jibril over wind and armies, Mika'il over rain and plants, the Angel of Death over the seizing of souls, and Israfil who delivers the command to them.2,3 Al-Sa'di widens the scope further, to rain, trees, seas, embryos, animals, Paradise and Hellfire.5 Mufti Shafi' ties this verse to the reward and punishment that await the soul already in the grave, citing a long tradition on the subject, while Israr Ahmad reads it as the angels carrying each soul to Sijjin or 'Illiyyin.7,8 A minority report even attributes this management to the seven celestial bodies, whose movements God has linked to change in worldly affairs.3

Grammatically, the sentence that begins the surah never states what the oath is sworn for; that response is left out and supplied by the commentators as an affirmation that resurrection and reckoning will happen, matching similar oaths elsewhere in the Qur'an.2,3,8,9,12,13 Al-Tanṭāwī notes that many hold all five descriptions to be one single group, the angels, at different tasks, closer to what is transmitted from the earliest generations, even though a wide range of other readings has also come down.9

Sayyid Qutb's own reflection is that whichever of these readings one takes, the Qur'an's aim in this string of oaths is to stir the listener's awareness and put them on alert before the greater event described next, and that chasing the exact identity of every word is not the point of reading it.6

79:42.title: The Hour Belongs to Allah Alone

79:42.essay_html:
The disbelievers of Makka ask about the Hour: when will it finally happen. The commentators say this was not honest curiosity. It was mockery from people who denied resurrection altogether.1,3,9,13 The word used for its arrival, mursaha, pictures a ship coming to rest at anchor: the Hour will appear and become fixed, the way a ship's voyage ends at its mooring point.1,2,3,12 One suggestion is that the Day is called 'the Hour' because it comes suddenly, or because its reckoning is swift, or because however long it lasts, it is a short span before Allah.9

The reply to this question is sharp: 'what do you have to do with mentioning it'. Reports say the Prophet ﷺ himself used to wonder and speak about the Hour often, until this verse came down telling him the matter was not his to pursue.1,3 The commentators explain that knowing the exact moment would bring no benefit, religious or worldly, to him or to anyone else.2,5,9,8,14 Some read the rebuke differently: it falls not on the Prophet ﷺ but on the questioners themselves, who spoke to him as though he held special knowledge, much as another verse says 'they ask you as if you were well informed about it'.3,9 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads the exchange as exposing their own foolishness: the matter is too immense for such a question, and the timing belongs to the Prophet's Lord, not to him.6 Mufti Muhammad Shafi (d. 1976) and Israr Ahmad (d. 2010) add that the demand itself was pointless, since this knowledge is Allah's own reserved matter, given to no angel and no prophet. The Prophet ﷺ was sent to warn and to give good news, not to fix a date.7,8

'To your Lord is its final point' settles where that knowledge lies: with Allah alone, not with any creature.1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,11,12,14 The commentators link this to two other verses that say the same thing plainly, that the knowledge of the Hour is with Allah.1,9 Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) reports that when Jibrīl عليه السلام asked the Prophet ﷺ this very question, he answered, 'the one questioned about it knows no more than the questioner', a report Abū Bakr Zakariyyā notes is found in Bukhārī.4,11 Al-Saʿdī (d. 1957) adds a reason for the concealment: people gain nothing, in this life or the next, from knowing the date. The real benefit lies precisely in it staying hidden, so Allah kept that knowledge for Himself.5

What remains for the Prophet ﷺ, then, is only to warn. 'You are only the warner of whoever fears it' fixes his task: deliver the warning, and leave what was never given to him to know.1,9,13,11,12,14,8 The warning is named for those who fear the Hour because they are the ones who take it to heart and benefit from it, even though the Prophet's message reaches everyone. Whoever fears will follow him and succeed; whoever denies only harms himself, a pattern the commentators compare to another verse: 'you only warn one who follows the reminder and fears the Most Merciful unseen'.3,4,9,12 On a small point of recitation, the word for 'warner' is read two ways, with or without tanwīn, both accepted by the reciters of the major cities.1,2,3 Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273) draws out a further point from the verse: it stands against anyone who claims the Hereafter's states are not truly felt in the body, but only a comfort or pain of the soul without any real sensation.3

The question of when is closed off entirely: that knowledge ends with Allah, and the Prophet ﷺ was sent only to warn those whose hearts already fear what is coming.1,3,4,9

79:46.essay_html:
The verse closes the sūrah by describing how the Hour will feel once it actually arrives. "It" is the Hour itself, and "they" are the deniers who once doubted it, identified by al-Baghawī as the disbelievers among the Quraysh.1,2,3,4,9,13,14

The point is not about calendars but about feeling. When these people finally see the Hour with their own eyes, its sheer terror and magnitude will make their entire worldly life shrink in memory to something as brief as one evening, or the morning before it.1,3,9 Qatādah put it simply: this is how the length of the world will look in their eyes once they have witnessed the Hereafter.1

Commentators differ on exactly what is being measured. Some take the "tarrying" to mean their whole span of worldly life; others take it to mean the time they lay in their graves before being raised.2,3,9 Ibn Kathīr reads it as the moment they rise from their graves toward the place of gathering, feeling that their stay had been no longer than one afternoon.4 A report reaching back to Ibn ʿAbbās gives it even more plainly: they will feel they had not stayed more than a single day.3

The wording itself carries a small grammatical puzzle. An evening (ʿashiyyah) does not, strictly, have a forenoon (ḍuḥā) of its own, since morning and evening belong to different halves of the day. Al-Farrāʾ pointed this out, but noted that ordinary Arabic speech joins them anyway, the way someone might say "I will come in the evening, or its morning" simply to mean the first or last part of a day. A line of poetry, "the evening of the new moon, or its darkest night," was cited as an even bolder instance of the same habit of speech.1,2,3 Al-Zamakhsharī, as relayed by al-Ṭanṭāwī, asked why the forenoon is attached to the evening at all, and answered that the two belong to one and the same day, and the phrasing is there to show that their stay felt like less than a full day, just a portion of it.9 Some commentators mark out the two stretches precisely: ʿashiyyah running from midday to sunset, and ḍuḥā from sunrise to midday, a definition traced back to Ibn ʿAbbās.4,9,12,13 The same image appears in Sūrat al-Aḥqāf, where the deniers likewise feel they had tarried no more than "an hour of the day" (46:35).2,3,9

Several commentators draw out what this shrinking means for how a person should regard the world. Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads it as exposing a great foolishness: people fight, oppress, and disobey for the sake of a life that will itself, in the end, look no bigger than an evening or a morning, while giving up an eternal Paradise for it.6 Isrār Aḥmad and Rebar make a similar point in their own words, that even a life of many years will feel, on that Day, like a few hours of one day, so the world carries little real weight against what is everlasting.8,14 Ahsanul Bayaan adds that once the disbelievers witness Hell's punishment, all memory of worldly comfort will vanish, leaving only the sense of a life barely lived.12 Abu Bakr Zakaria notes that this theme of life's brevity recurs across the Qurʾān, in Yūnus, al-Isrāʾ, Ṭā Hā, al-Muʾminūn, al-Rūm, Yā Sīn and al-Aḥqāf.11 Wahiduddin Khan frames the underlying test as a choice between the visible present world and the hidden Hereafter, one that calls for restraining the self's desires rather than turning arrogant.10

Whichever moment is being measured, the grave or the world, the sense left by every reading is the same: what looked immense while it was being lived will, on that Day, seem no longer than an evening, or its morning.1,3,4,9

79:27.title: The Sky and Earth as Proof
79:27.in_short: Facing people who mock the idea of being raised after death, the passage points to the sky and the earth: raising the vast heavens, darkening its night and lighting its day, spreading the earth, drawing out water and pasture, and fixing the mountains, are all far greater feats than remaking a human body — so remaking you is not the hard part.

claims.text: The question 'are you harder to create, or the sky?' is addressed to the Meccans who denied resurrection; it is a rebuke. If building the heavens is the greater feat, then re-creating a human being — a lesser thing — cannot be beyond the same power. The point echoes other Qur'anic verses making the same argument (e.g. 'the creation of the heavens and earth is greater than the creation of mankind', and 'is not the One who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?').
'He built it' (banāhā) means He raised the sky and made it a ceiling or roof over the earth.

original_terms.gloss: He built/raised it (as a ceiling)

claims.text: 'He raised its height' (rafaʿa samkahā) describes lifting the sky's structure high into space; 'and levelled it' (fa-sawwāhā) means He made it perfectly even, with no cracks, flaws or fissures in it.

original_terms.gloss: height, structure raised aloft

claims.text: The sky is like one interlocking structure: its stars and orbits are bound together so that nothing strays or collides. Reflecting closely on this coherence, Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) says, leaves the mind unable to explain it except by acknowledging a directing power behind it.
'He darkened its night' (aghṭasha laylahā) means He made the night dark; 'and brought out its morning brightness' (akhraja ḍuḥāhā) means He revealed and lit up its day.

original_terms.gloss: made dark
its morning brightness

claims.text: Night and morning-light are grammatically attached to 'the sky' (its night, its brightness) because sunset and sunrise — the cause of darkness and light — belong to the sky.
The word ḍuḥā (forenoon brightness) rather than nahār (day) is used because the forenoon hour is reckoned the finest part of the day.
The night was darkened so that people could rest in it, and the day was made bright so that people could go about seeking provision and trade.

Commentators differ on 'baʿda dhālika' (after that). One reading takes it literally: the earth's spreading-out truly came after the sky's creation — a view traced to Ibn ʿAbbās and preferred by al-Ṭabarī, and also held by Ibn Kathīr. A second reading takes 'baʿda' to mean 'together with' (maʿa), as in the phrase 'coarse, and moreover (baʿda dhālika) ignoble' (68:13), so the verse would not be fixing a strict sequence.

original_terms.gloss: after that / (alternatively) together with that

claims.text: 'Dahāhā' (He spread it) means He flattened and extended the earth, made clear by what follows — bringing forth its water and pasture. One gloss describes it as Allah depositing the earth's benefits within it.

original_terms.gloss: He spread/flattened it out

claims.text: To reconcile this verse with others that mention the earth's creation before the sky (as in 2:29 and the earlier passage in Sūrat al-Sajdah), the resolution offered is: the earth's raw substance was created first, but its 'spreading out' — being made fit for habitation, having its water and pasture drawn out, and its mountains anchored — came after the heaven's creation. Ibn Kathīr calls this Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation and says it was al-Ṭabarī's preferred view.

A minority gloss, attributed to Ibn Zayd, takes 'dahāhā' to mean He 'ploughed' or 'split' the earth (from a root meaning to cleave), linking it to another verse describing the earth being split open for produce to grow.
'He brought forth from it its water and its pasture' means He caused springs, rivers and seas to flow from the earth, and made vegetation grow for grazing.

Al-Qurṭubī cites al-Qutaybī's observation that these two things, water and pasture, stand in for everything the earth produces: food and goods of every kind — herbage, trees, grain, dates, fodder, firewood, clothing, fire (from wood) and salt (from water).

Using modern scientific description, the water now on earth is said to have originated from the earth itself: the early earth was a molten ball; as it cooled, vapours formed an atmosphere; hydrogen and oxygen combined to make water, which fell as rain for ages, eventually giving rise to what is now called the water cycle.
'The mountains He anchored' means He fixed them firmly in the earth so that it would not shake or tremble with those living on it.

A report traced through al-Ṭabarī, via ʿAlī, states that when Allah created the earth, it shook and protested that Adam's offspring would be set upon it, casting their filth and sins on it; so Allah anchored it with mountains, some visible and some not, and its first settling was likened to the quivering of a slaughtered camel's flesh.

report.graded_by: not graded by al-Ṭabarī in the source given

claims.text: 'A benefit for you and your livestock' (matāʿan lakum wa li-anʿāmikum) means all this — the water, the pasture, the anchored mountains — is provision granted for people and their animals to enjoy for the span of this worldly life.

original_terms.gloss: provision, a thing to be enjoyed

claims.text: Grammatically, 'matāʿan' stands as an accusative verbal noun (maṣdar) implying an unstated verb, as if the sentence read 'so that you may enjoy it, an enjoyment.'

The scale of the universe on display is so vast that everything else appears small by comparison. Since an event of this magnitude has already occurred in the world, there is no reason a comparatively small event — resurrection — could not also occur.

Reflecting on the earth's night, day, spreading, water, pasture and mountains together, Sayyid Qutb links this precise ordering of the cosmos — matched against modern accounts of the earth's cooling and formation — to an argument against mere chance: such a precisely working system could not have arisen by accident, and this points on to the reality that the same order and purpose extends to human resurrection and requital.

79:27.essay_html:
The passage answers people who mocked the idea of being raised after death. The question put to them is a rebuke: is creating you harder, or creating the sky? Since building the heavens is plainly the greater feat, remaking a human body afterwards cannot be beyond the same power. Commentators link this to other verses making the same point, that the creation of the heavens and earth is greater than the creation of mankind.1,2,3,4,7,9,11,12,13,14 Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021) puts it plainly: the universe on display is so vast that everything else looks small beside it, so a comparatively small event like resurrection should pose no difficulty once a far bigger one has already happened.10

'He built it' means Allah raised the sky and made it a ceiling over the earth.1,2,3,9,13 'He raised its height' (samk) describes lifting its structure high, and 'levelled it' means He made it perfectly even, without cracks or flaws.1,2,3,4,5,9,12,13 Sayyid Qutb (d. 1966) reflects that the sky holds together like one interlocking structure, its stars and orbits bound so that nothing strays or collides, a coherence he says leaves the mind no way to explain it except by acknowledging a directing power behind it.6

'He darkened its night' means He made the night dark, and 'brought out its morning brightness' means He lit up the day.1,2,3,4,5,9,11,12,13,14 Night and morning-light are spoken of as belonging to the sky, since sunset and sunrise, which cause them, occur there.1,2,3,9 One note explains why 'ḍuḥā' (forenoon brightness) is chosen over the plainer word for 'day': the forenoon is reckoned the finest hour.12 Another adds a purpose: the night was darkened so people could rest, the day lit up so they could go about seeking their provision.14

The phrase 'and the earth, after that, He spread out' has drawn two readings. One takes 'after' literally: the earth's spreading came after the sky's creation, a view traced to Ibn ʿAbbās and preferred by al-Ṭabarī (d. 923), also held by Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373).1,4,9,14 The other reads 'after' as meaning 'together with', as in the Qur'an's use of the same word elsewhere, so that no strict sequence is being fixed.1,2,3,9,14 The commentators reconcile this with verses that place the earth's creation before the sky's: the earth's raw substance came first, but its 'spreading' — being made fit to live on, its water and pasture drawn out, its mountains anchored — came after the heaven was made.4,5,9,11,12,14 A minority gloss takes 'spread' instead to mean 'ploughed' or 'split', tying it to a verse about the earth being opened for produce.1

'He brought forth its water and its pasture' means He caused springs, rivers and seas to flow, and made vegetation grow for grazing.1,2,3,9,13,14 Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273) relays that these two things stand for everything the earth yields: herbage, trees, grain, dates, fodder, firewood, clothing, fire and salt.3 Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) reads this alongside a modern account of the earth's history: a molten ball cooling, releasing vapours that formed an atmosphere, in which hydrogen and oxygen combined into water that fell as rain over ages until the water cycle we now describe took shape.8 'The mountains He anchored' means He fixed them firmly so the earth would not shake with its inhabitants.1,2,3,4,9,13,14 Al-Ṭabarī relays a report through ʿAlī رضي الله عنه that the earth trembled at its own creation, fearing what mankind would do upon it, until Allah steadied it with mountains, some seen and some hidden; the report is left ungraded in the source.1

All of this, the verses close, is 'a provision for you and your livestock': the water, the pasture, the firm mountains, are benefits granted for the span of this worldly life.1,2,3,4,9,13 Grammatically, al-Qurṭubī notes 'matāʿan' stands for an implied verb, as though the sentence read 'so that you may enjoy it, an enjoyment'.3 Qutb draws the whole picture together: night, day, the spread earth, its water, pasture and mountains, form too precise and ordered a system to be an accident, and this precision, he argues, carries the mind on to the reality that the same order and purpose stands behind resurrection and requital.6

The commentators read this stretch as one sustained comparison: the One who raised the sky without flaw, darkened its night and lit its day, spread the earth and drew water, pasture and mountains from it for the sake of people and their animals, cannot find it hard to bring the same people back to life.

79:34.title: The Great Overwhelming Event
79:34.in_short: This passage describes the Day of Judgement itself: man will remember everything he did, Hell will be uncovered for all to see, and people will split into two kinds — those who rebelled and chased this life, who end in Hell, and those who feared standing before their Lord and reined in their desires, who end in Paradise.

claims.text: The 'Greatest Overwhelming Event' (al-Ṭāmmah al-Kubrā) refers to the Day of Resurrection, linked by several commentators to the second trumpet-blast that brings about the raising of the dead.

original_terms.gloss: the greatest overwhelming calamity, a name for the Day of Judgement

claims.text: Linguistically, 'Ṭāmmah' comes from a root meaning to overwhelm or flood, describing a calamity so great it swallows up every other disaster and dwarfs it.
Al-Qasim ibn al-Walid and Mujahid are reported to describe the Greatest Event as the moment the people of Paradise are driven to Paradise and the people of Hell are driven to Hell.

Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ frames the section as a whole: the coming verses show every person's deeds presented, describe the two abodes, and give traits by which a person may judge, as a general rule, where he is heading — noting that exceptions exist through intercession or divine grace.
On that Day man will recall everything he did in the world, both good and evil.

Al-Saʿdī describes the intensity of that recollection: a man will wish for even the weight of an atom more good deed, and grieve over the weight of an atom of added sin. He then realises that his entire profit or loss rested on what he did in this life, and every worldly tie is cut except his deeds.
Ibn Kathīr cross-references verse 89:23, that man will remember, but asks 'of what avail will the remembrance be to him' — the recollection comes too late to help.
Isrār Aḥmad links this remembrance to the people described in Sūrat al-Kahf (18:104) whose striving was lost in worldly life while they believed they were doing well.
Hell will be brought out and displayed openly for every onlooker to see, with no concealment left.
Mujahid and Ibn ʿAbbās are reported as saying the veil is removed from Hell so that all creation looks upon it.
A variant reading, 'tura' (you see, second person), is noted; on this reading the address is to the Prophet ﷺ but the meaning is general to people.

Commentators differ on who precisely 'sees' Hell here: some say it is specifically the disbeliever, since he is the one thrown into it; others say the believer sees it too, so as to recognise the value of the blessing of being spared, while the disbeliever is the one who actually burns in it.

Sayyid Quṭb notes that the word 'burrizat' (brought out) carries intensification both in its grammatical form and in its meaning, bringing the scene before every eye; this is the Day when every person's fate becomes distinct and Allah's whole system of trial in the first life is laid open.
'Ṭaghā' (transgressed) is explained as exceeding bounds — rebelling against and disobeying one's Lord, being arrogant in disbelief.
'Preferred the worldly life' means giving the fleeting pleasure of this world precedence over religion and the Hereafter, abandoning deeds for the next life in favour of striving for this one.
A report links these verses to al-Naḍr and his son al-Ḥārith, though the verse is understood as general, covering every disbeliever who prefers this world over the next.

Reports are cited warning against preferring worldly life over religion: Ḥudhayfah رضي الله عنه is said to have feared this most for the community, and a further report 'found in the books' attributes to Allah a warning that whoever prefers his worldly life to his Hereafter will have his cares scattered upon him.

report.graded_by: al-Qurṭubī notes it without a stated chain of authentication

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb reads 'ṭughyān' (transgression) broadly: it is not limited to political tyranny by the powerful, but applies to anyone who strays from the path of guidance and truth. Its chief mark is preferring this world over the next without regard for being held to account.
Hell (al-Jaḥīm) will be his dwelling, his final destination, the place he returns to.
Ibn Kathīr adds that such a person's food there will be from the tree of Zaqqūm and his drink from Ḥamīm (scalding water).
'Fearing the standing (maqām) of his Lord' is explained as fearing the appearance before Allah on the Day of Reckoning, standing before Him for judgement.
Mujahid is reported to explain this fear as one felt in this world, at the very moment of being drawn toward a sin, that recalls the standing for reckoning and so makes a person desist.
'Restrained the self from desire' (hawā) means holding the soul back from the forbidden things it craves.

Sahl is reported to have said that abandoning desire is the key to Paradise, citing this verse; Ibn Masʿūd رضي الله عنه is reported to have warned of a time when desire leads truth rather than truth leading desire.

Several occasion-of-revelation reports are given for these two verses: that they concern Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr رضي الله عنه, who shielded the Prophet ﷺ at Uḥud until pierced by arrows, and his brother ʿĀmir; or that they concern Abū Jahl against Muṣʿab; or that they were revealed about Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq رضي الله عنه, over food he learned had come from soothsaying and which he then made himself vomit up.

report.graded_by: al-Qurṭubī relays multiple reports without adjudicating between them

claims.text: Paradise will be his dwelling place.

Sayyid Quṭb argues the two conditions for Paradise belong together because it is Allah, the Creator of the human self, who alone knows both its weakness and its cure. Man is not commanded to have no desire at all, but to bridle it.

Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ, citing Qāḍī Thanāʾullāh Pānīpatī's Tafsīr Maẕharī, sets out three levels of restraining the self from desire: first, avoiding beliefs contrary to the clear texts and the consensus of the predecessors (the baseline for a Muslim); second, the middle level, remembering one's accountability before Allah and abstaining even from doubtful matters, citing the hadith of Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr رضي الله عنه on doubtful things; third, the highest level, where through remembrance and struggle the pull of desire is removed altogether, the station of divine closeness (walāyah).

report.graded_by: Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ, citing the hadith of Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr without grading it here

claims.text: Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ notes that the verse's two conditions for Paradise are, in effect, one: fear of standing before Allah is what produces the restraint of desire.

Wahiduddin Khan reads the pair of verses as describing man standing between two realms: the visible present world and the hidden Hereafter. The real test is to prefer the Hereafter, which takes the courage to control base desire and not behave arrogantly.

One reading of 'the standing of his Lord' gives it two possible senses: fear of appearing before the Lord for reckoning, or contemplation of the Lord's majestic station which itself restrains a person from sin and from following desire — both meanings are held to be valid.

79:34.essay_html:
The passage opens with the 'Greatest Overwhelming Event' (al-Ṭāmmah al-Kubrā), understood as the Day of Resurrection itself, tied by some to the second trumpet-blast that raises the dead.1,2,3,4,13 The word itself, commentators note, comes from a root meaning to overwhelm or flood — a calamity so great it swallows every other disaster.1,2,3,9,11 One report describes it as the moment the people of Paradise are driven to Paradise and the people of Hell driven to Hell.1,3 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ frames what follows as a general description: deeds presented, two abodes described, and traits by which a person may judge, as a rule, which way he is heading — though exceptions remain possible through intercession or grace.7

On that Day, man remembers everything he did, good and evil.1,2,4,5,9,13,14 Al-Saʿdī pictures the intensity of it: a man will wish for even the weight of an atom more good deed, and grieve over an atom's weight of added sin, realising that his whole profit or loss rested on what he did in life, every worldly bond now cut except his deeds.5 Ibn Kathīr links this to another verse, that man will remember, 'but of what avail will the remembrance be to him' — it comes too late to help.4 Isrār Aḥmad connects it to the people in Sūrat al-Kahf whose striving was wasted in this life while they believed they were doing well.8

Hell is then brought out, exposed for every onlooker to see, with nothing hidden.1,2,3,4,5,9,13,14 Mujahid and Ibn ʿAbbās are said to describe the veil being lifted so all creation looks on it.2,3 Commentators differ on exactly who 'sees' it: some say the disbeliever specifically, since he is the one cast into it, others say the believer too, so he recognises the value of the mercy that spared him, while the disbeliever is the one who actually burns.3,12 Sayyid Quṭb points to the intensified form of the word 'brought out', noting it places the scene before every eye — this is the Day each person's fate becomes distinct, and Allah's whole design of testing in the first life stands revealed.6

People then divide in two. The one who 'transgressed' (ṭaghā) is the one who exceeded bounds, rebelling against and disobeying his Lord in arrogance.1,2,9,13,14 Sayyid Quṭb reads this broadly: not only political tyranny by the powerful, but anyone who strays from guidance and truth, whose defining mark is preferring this world over the next without a thought for being held to account.6 'Preferring the worldly life' means giving fleeting pleasure precedence over religion and the Hereafter, abandoning work for the next life to chase this one.1,4,5,7,9 One report ties this to al-Naḍr and his son, though the verse is taken as general, covering every disbeliever who makes this choice.3 Reports are also cited warning of this danger — Ḥudhayfah's رضي الله عنه fear for the community, and an unattributed saying warning that whoever prefers his worldly life to his Hereafter will have his cares scattered upon him.3 For such a person, Hell is the dwelling, the final return, with food from the tree of Zaqqūm and drink of scalding water, as Ibn Kathīr adds.1,3,4,9,13

The other kind is the one who 'feared the standing of his Lord' and 'restrained the self from desire'. The fear is explained as fear of appearing before Allah for reckoning.1,2,3,5,9,13 Mujahid is reported to locate this fear in the very moment of temptation in this life, the fear that makes a person turn back from sin.2,3 Restraining the self from hawā (desire, base craving) means holding the soul back from what it wants but Allah forbids.1,2,3,5,9,13,14 Sahl is reported to have called abandoning desire the key to Paradise, and Ibn Masʿūd رضي الله عنه warned of a time when desire leads truth rather than the reverse.3 Various occasion-of-revelation reports are attached here — to Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr رضي الله عنه, who shielded the Prophet ﷺ at Uḥud until pierced by arrows, to Abū Jahl set against him, or to Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq رضي الله عنه over food he learned was tainted and made himself vomit up.3 Sayyid Quṭb reads the two conditions as one thing seen from two sides: only the Creator of the self knows its weakness and its cure, and man is not asked to have no desire at all, only to bridle it.6 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ, citing the Tafsīr Maẕharī, sets out three levels of that restraint — holding to sound belief, remembering accountability enough to avoid even doubtful matters, and finally, through remembrance and struggle, reaching a state where the pull of desire is removed altogether7 — and notes that, looked at closely, the two conditions collapse into one: it is fear of Allah that produces the restraint.7 Wahiduddin Khan frames the whole pair as man standing between the visible present world and the hidden Hereafter, the real test being the courage to prefer the unseen.10 For this person, Paradise is the dwelling.1,3,5,9,13

Two fears, two abodes: one who feared nothing and chased this world finds Hell waiting as he saw it; one who feared standing before his Lord and reined in his own desire finds Paradise as his home.

79:6.title: The Two Blasts and the Rising
79:6.in_short: This passage describes the instant the Hour breaks: two great shocks, one after another, followed by hearts frozen in fear and eyes cast down. The deniers who once mocked resurrection are shown asking, in disbelief, whether they can really be brought back after turning to dust, only to find themselves standing on open ground after a single blast.

claims.text: The Rajifah and the Radifah are most commonly read as the two blasts of the Trumpet: the first kills every living thing, the second brings the dead back to life.

original_terms.gloss: the shaking/quaking one, i.e. the first trumpet-blast
the following one, i.e. the second trumpet-blast

claims.text: An alternate reading takes the Rajifah as the earth and mountains shaking, and the Radifah as a second event, either the Hour itself or the sky splitting apart in a single crushing.
Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads the first shock as the earth's own trembling and the second as the sky's trembling and splitting, since elsewhere the Qur'an ties the word 'rajf' explicitly to the earth.
A report has the Prophet پرٰفار rising in the last part of the night to say, 'The Rajifah has come, followed by the Radifah, death has come with what it brings.'

report.graded_by: not graded in the sources provided

claims.text: A further report, attributed to the Prophet ﷺ via Qatādah, states that forty (years) separate the two blasts.

report.graded_by: not graded in the sources provided

claims.text: Wahīduddīn Khān (d. 2021) draws a parallel with the yearly cycle of nature: dry, barren land bursting into green life after a storm shows, in nature's own language, that the Hereafter emerging from this world is just as possible.

Grammarians debated where the reply to the oath sworn at the start of the surah actually falls: some hold it is left unstated and understood from context (supported by the deniers' own words later in the passage), some locate it in this verse itself or elsewhere in the surah, and some see a rearrangement of the wording.
'Hearts will tremble' (qulūbun wājifah) is read by most commentators as hearts gripped by fear.

original_terms.gloss: trembling, quaking with fear

claims.text: Al-Suddī read 'wājifah' instead as hearts 'displaced from where they sit,' comparing it to the verse describing hearts rising to the throat.
Other grammarians described the same state with near-synonyms: restless and unsettled (al-Mu'arrij), or convulsed (al-Mubarrid).
The root of 'wājifah' is tied to a quickened heartbeat, the same word used for the fast gait of a horse or camel breaking into a run.
'Eyes will be downcast' (khāshi'ah) is glossed as eyes made humble and disgraced by the terror they witness.

original_terms.gloss: humbled, downcast in disgrace

claims.text: Grammatically, 'hearts' (qulūb) is the subject with 'trembling' as its adjective, while 'their eyes are downcast' forms the predicate that completes the sentence.

Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010) notes that these trembling hearts and downcast eyes belong to those who denied the resurrection in this life; believers, by contrast, are described elsewhere as untouched by the greatest terror.
The deniers' question, 'shall we be returned to al-ḥāfirah,' is most often read as 'returned to life as we first were,' their way of expressing scornful disbelief at resurrection.

original_terms.gloss: the first state, one's original condition before death

claims.text: Others take al-ḥāfirah as the dug earth of the grave itself, so the question becomes 'shall we be returned alive inside our own graves.'
Others again take al-ḥāfirah as one of the names of the Fire, on the authority of Ibn Zayd (and Muqātil and Zayd b. Aslam per Qurṭubī).
Ibn 'Abbās رضي الله عنه is also reported to have taken al-ḥāfirah as meaning this present world, according to Qurṭubī.
The word al-ḥāfirah is tied to an old Arabic idiom, 'he returned by the way he came,' supported by cited poetry.
The bones described as 'nakhirah' (or 'nākhirah' in another recitation) are read either as bones crumbled to dust, or as bones so hollowed out that the wind makes a sound passing through them.

original_terms.gloss: decayed and crumbling bone / hollow bone through which wind whistles

claims.text: Al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) judged 'nakhirah' the more common and eloquent of the two readings, though he leaned toward 'nākhirah' because it matches the end-rhyme of the surrounding verses.
Their verdict, 'that would be a losing return,' is read as fear that being brought back to life would only deliver them to punishment, so the return itself ends in loss.

original_terms.gloss: a return that ends in loss

claims.text: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is reported to have read 'khāsirah' here as meaning the return is simply false and will never happen, rather than a return they fear will bring them loss.
Against their disbelief, the answer is that it will take nothing but a single blast (zajrah wāḥidah), showing how effortless resurrection is for God.

original_terms.gloss: a single rebuking shout/blast

claims.text: Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) ties this ease to other Qur'anic verses describing God's command as swift as the twinkling of an eye, and notes all people, first and last, will stand looking when Isrāfīl blows the Trumpet.
Sayyid Quṭb notes that the word chosen is 'zajrah,' a harsh rebuking shout, rather than the plain word for a cry, because it matches the severity of the whole scene described in the surah.
'As-Sāhirah,' where they suddenly find themselves, is read by most commentators as simply the open surface of the earth, after they had lain within it.

original_terms.gloss: the open surface/plain of the earth

claims.text: The name is explained from 'sahar' (wakefulness), since living things both sleep and stay wakeful on the surface of the earth, a reading supported by a line of pre-Islamic poetry describing 'the flesh of the sāhirah and the sea.'
Mujāhid took as-sāhirah instead as simply 'a level place'; Ibn Kathīr adds that people will be brought up from the earth's lowest depths to its highest ground.
Some named as-sāhirah as an actual location: a tract of land between Mount Ḥassān and Mount Arīḥā in Syria, a mountain beside Jerusalem, or the land of Syria generally.
Qatādah is reported to have taken as-sāhirah as Hellfire itself, meaning the deniers will find themselves in the Fire.
Al-Rabī' b. Anas linked this verse to other passages describing the earth being changed into another earth and mountains being levelled flat.

Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976) reads sāhirah as the levelled, mountain-less surface of the re-created earth, and notes that the Prophet ﷺ, hurt by the stubbornness of those who mocked resurrection, is next consoled by the story of Mūsā عليه السلام and Fir'awn, showing earlier prophets faced the same rejection.

79:6.essay_html:
This passage describes the instant the Hour breaks. Two great shocks arrive one after the other, hearts and eyes are overwhelmed, and the deniers of resurrection are shown mocking the very thing about to happen to them.

The Rajifah and the Radifah are read by most commentators as the two blasts of the Trumpet: the first kills every living thing, the second brings the dead back to life.1,2,3,4,9,13 Some report the two blasts stand roughly forty years apart, attributed to a saying of the Prophet ﷺ.1,2,3 Others take the Rajifah as the earth and mountains shaking, and the Radifah as a second shock, either the Hour itself or the sky splitting apart.1,2,3 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads the first shock as the earth's own trembling and the second as the sky's, since the Qur'an elsewhere ties this word directly to the earth.6 A report has the Prophet ﷺ rising in the night to say, "the Rajifah has come, followed by the Radifah, death has come with what it brings."1,2,3,11 Wahīduddīn Khān (d. 2021) draws a parallel with the yearly cycle: dry, dead land bursting into green life after a storm hints, in nature's own language, that a life after this one is no less possible.10

Grammarians also debated where the reply to the oath sworn earlier in the surah actually lands. Some hold it is left unstated and understood from what follows, others place it in this verse or elsewhere in the surah, and some see a rearrangement of the wording.1,3

"Hearts will tremble" (qulūbun wājifah) is read by most as hearts gripped by fear.1,2,3,4,5,9,13 Al-Suddī read it instead as hearts "displaced from where they sit," comparing it to the verse that speaks of hearts rising to the throat.2,3 Other grammarians described the same state as restless and unsettled, or convulsed.3 The root of wājifah ties to a quickened heartbeat, the same word used for the fast gait of a running horse.2,3 "Eyes will be downcast" (khāshiʿah) is glossed as humbled and disgraced by the terror they witness.1,2,3,4,5,8,9 Grammatically, "hearts" is the subject with "trembling" as its description, and "their eyes are downcast" completes the sentence as its predicate.3 Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010) notes these trembling hearts belong to those who denied the resurrection in life; believers, by contrast, are told elsewhere that the greatest terror will not touch them.9

The deniers' question, "shall we be returned to al-ḥāfirah," is read most often as "returned to life as we first were," their way of mocking the very idea of resurrection.1,2,3,4,9 Others take al-ḥāfirah as the dug earth of the grave itself, so the question becomes "shall we be returned alive inside our graves."1,2,3 Others again take it as one of the names of the Fire, or as this present life.1,2,3 The word is tied to an old Arabic phrase, "he returned by the way he came."1,3 Their "decayed bones" (read as nakhirah or nākhirah) means bones crumbled to dust, or bones so hollowed that wind passing through them makes a sound.1,2,3,4,9 Al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) judged nakhirah the more common and eloquent of the two words, though he leaned toward nākhirah since it matches the rhyme of the surrounding verses.1

Their own verdict, "that would be a losing return," is read as their fear that being brought back to life will only deliver them to punishment, so the return itself is a loss.1,2,3,4,9 Al-Ḥasan read "losing" here as meaning the return will never actually happen at all, a return that is false and futile.3 Against all their disbelief, the answer comes at once: it will take nothing but a single blast (zajrah wāḥidah), showing how effortless resurrection is for God.1,2,5,9,13 Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) ties this ease to other verses describing God's command as swift as the blink of an eye.4 Sayyid Quṭb notes that the word chosen is zajrah, a harsh rebuking shout, rather than a plain cry, because it matches the severity of the whole scene.6

"As-Sāhirah," where they suddenly find themselves, is read by most as simply the open surface of the earth, after they had lain within it.1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,11,13,14 The name is explained from sahar, wakefulness, since living things both sleep and wake upon the earth's surface, a reading supported by a line of pre-Islamic poetry.1,2,3,9 Mujāhid took it instead as simply "a level place," with Ibn Kathīr adding that people will be brought up from the earth's depths to its highest ground.1,4 Some named it as an actual location: a tract of land in Syria, a mountain beside Jerusalem, or the general land of Syria.1,2,3 Qatādah took it as Hellfire itself.1,2,3 Al-Rabīʿ b. Anas linked the verse to other passages describing the earth remade and mountains levelled flat.4 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976) reads sāhirah as the levelled, mountain-less surface of the re-created earth, and notes that the Prophet ﷺ, hurt by the stubbornness of those who mocked resurrection, is next consoled by the story of Mūsā عليه السلام and Firʿawn, a reminder that earlier prophets faced the same rejection.7

Across all these readings, the commentators keep returning to the same point held up against the deniers' scorn: what strikes them as impossible costs their Maker nothing more than a single blast.1,4,5,9
